actors.name: GE Vernova
actors.role: makes the gas turbines and grid equipment that new data centres need for power
actors.advantage: One of three makers of large gas turbines, with the order book full: a $197bn backlog of equipment and long-term service contracts, 122 GW of gas backlog and slot reservations, and orders up 96% in Q3 2026. A turbine factory takes years to expand, so buyers queue for its output and pay for service for decades.
actors.desire: Turn the power rush into a multi-year backlog at rising prices.
actors.fear: A pause in data-centre building, or cheaper paths to power (solar with storage, small reactors) once its backlog is delivered.

actors.name: Siemens Energy
actors.role: Europe's maker of gas turbines and high-voltage grid equipment; the other large-turbine source besides GE Vernova and Mitsubishi Heavy
actors.advantage: It is one of the few firms that can build large gas turbines and grid transformers, so it shares in the same power rush; its edge over GE Vernova is grid technology more than turbine volume.
actors.desire: Win data-centre and grid orders at better margins.
actors.fear: A demand pause, and execution problems of the kind its wind unit had.

actors.name: Vertiv
actors.role: supplies the power distribution and liquid cooling inside AI data centres
actors.advantage: Racks of GPUs need dense power and liquid cooling; Vertiv sells both at scale and designs them alongside NVIDIA's rack generations, so it is specified into most large builds.
actors.desire: Be designed into each new GPU generation's racks.
actors.fear: A capex pause, and rivals such as Schneider Electric and Eaton.

actors.name: Constellation
actors.role: the largest US nuclear operator, selling around-the-clock carbon-free power to data-centre buyers
actors.advantage: Existing nuclear plants are the scarcest firm, clean power, and new reactors take a decade to build. Constellation owns the largest fleet and signs 20-year contracts with hyperscalers.
actors.desire: Sign long contracts at premium prices for its reactors.
actors.fear: Regulators limiting data centres beside reactors; a demand pause.

actors.name: NextEra
actors.role: the largest US developer of wind, solar and storage, and Florida's regulated utility
actors.advantage: Development scale and a regulated utility's cheap capital let it add power fastest where the grid allows; it sells data centres new renewable and storage capacity.
actors.desire: Sell gigawatts of new power to data centres.
actors.fear: Grid interconnection queues, higher interest rates and subsidy cuts.

actors.name: Applied Mat.
actors.role: the largest maker of chipmaking equipment (deposition, etch, inspection)
actors.advantage: The broadest tool line in the industry and an installed base whose service and upgrades tie fabs to it; rivals match it tool by tool but not across the line.
actors.desire: Gain from gate-all-around transistors, backside power and advanced packaging.
actors.fear: Export limits on China and a capex pause by chipmakers.

actors.name: Lam Research
actors.role: leads etch and deposition tools, critical for memory and 3D structures
actors.advantage: Process know-how in high-aspect-ratio etch, which 3D NAND, DRAM and stacked HBM depend on; memory makers design around its tools.
actors.desire: Ride the memory build-out.
actors.fear: China limits and the end of the memory boom.

actors.name: Tokyo Electron
actors.role: Japan's chip-tool leader; its coater-developers run beside every lithography scanner
actors.advantage: A near-monopoly in the coater-developer tracks paired with EUV scanners, plus strong etch and deposition lines.
actors.desire: Hold the track monopoly into High-NA EUV.
actors.fear: Export alignment with US rules and a capex pause.

actors.name: KLA
actors.role: dominates process control: the inspection and metrology that find defects on wafers
actors.advantage: Yield at advanced nodes depends on finding defects early; KLA's inspection tools and their data libraries have no close rival.
actors.desire: Grow with every new node and packaging step.
actors.fear: China limits and a capex pause.

actors.name: Synopsys
actors.role: chip-design software (EDA) and IP; with Cadence it designs nearly every advanced chip
actors.advantage: Design flows, verified libraries and engineers trained on its tools make switching costly. The EDA duopoly is a quiet choke point that US rules can switch off for China.
actors.desire: Sell AI-driven design tools to every chip team.
actors.fear: Export rules cutting China, and customers' in-house tools.

actors.name: Cadence
actors.role: chip-design software and system simulation; Synopsys's duopoly partner
actors.advantage: Lock-in through design flows and engineers' training, shared with Synopsys; strong in analog, packaging and system simulation.
actors.desire: Sell design and simulation to every AI chip team.
actors.fear: Export rules cutting China.

actors.name: Arm
actors.role: licenses the instruction set behind nearly all phones and a growing share of data-centre CPUs (NVIDIA Grace, AWS Graviton, Google Axion)
actors.advantage: Network economies: the software ecosystem built for Arm makes it the default alternative to x86, and it earns royalties on every chip without making any.
actors.desire: Raise royalties as its designs move into AI data centres.
actors.fear: RISC-V, and licensees designing around it.

actors.name: SMIC
actors.role: China's leading foundry; it makes Huawei's Ascend chips without EUV
actors.advantage: State backing and a protected home market. It reaches 7nm-class chips with older DUV tools by multi-patterning, at lower yield and higher cost, and ranks third in foundry revenue.
actors.desire: Reach 5nm-class production without EUV.
actors.fear: Tighter tool controls, including the servicing of the DUV tools it has.

actors.name: CXMT
actors.role: China's largest DRAM maker, listed in Shanghai (688825.SS)
actors.advantage: State-backed scale in commodity DRAM inside China's protected market, and an HBM programme to supply Huawei. Its edge is environment (subsidy and a closed market) more than technology.
actors.desire: Supply China's AI chips with domestic memory, including HBM.
actors.fear: US controls on memory tools and a DRAM price collapse.

actors.name: Huawei
actors.advantage: A captive market and a full stack: Ascend chips, CANN software, and DeepSeek's V4 tuned to them. Policy shields it from NVIDIA; SMIC's output and HBM supply limit how much it can ship.

actors.name: Marvell
actors.role: designs custom AI chips for hyperscalers (AWS Trainium) and the optical links between accelerators
actors.advantage: Custom-silicon and electro-optics design teams for hyperscalers that want an alternative to Broadcom; a second design house rather than a platform.
actors.desire: Win more custom accelerator programmes.
actors.fear: Losing a programme to Broadcom or to in-house teams.

actors.name: Arista
actors.role: Ethernet switches for AI clusters
actors.advantage: High-speed Ethernet switching with software (EOS) trusted by Microsoft and Meta; Ethernet is displacing InfiniBand in many AI clusters.
actors.desire: Make Ethernet the fabric of AI.
actors.fear: NVIDIA's own Ethernet (Spectrum-X) and customers building white-box switches.

actors.name: Dell
actors.role: builds AI servers and racks for enterprises, GPU clouds and xAI
actors.advantage: Scale in server supply chains and enterprise sales; it resells NVIDIA's systems and keeps a thin margin of its own.
actors.desire: Be the enterprise's AI-factory vendor.
actors.fear: NVIDIA and the ODMs selling direct; thin margins.

actors.name: Foxconn
actors.role: assembles NVIDIA's rack-scale AI servers and Apple's iPhones: the world's largest electronics manufacturer
actors.advantage: Process power and scale in assembly; it builds NVIDIA's GB200 and GB300 racks at volume, but on thin margins set by its customers.
actors.desire: Move up from assembly to whole AI data-centre systems.
actors.fear: Customers moving assembly to rivals or to other countries; tariffs.

actors.name: Microsoft
actors.advantage: Microsoft owns the enterprise channel (Microsoft 365, Azure) and about 27 percent of OpenAI, and also sells Anthropic's Claude. Microsoft Cloud earns $63.9bn a quarter, and it funds about $170bn a year of capex while staying cash-flow positive.

actors.name: Amazon
actors.advantage: Two scale businesses: the largest e-commerce logistics network (more than 1.5 billion items delivered same-day or overnight in one quarter) and the largest cloud (AWS, $46.0bn a quarter, growing 39%), with its own Trainium chips to which Anthropic committed $100bn over ten years. Each funds the other, and rivals must match both.

actors.name: Meta
actors.role: Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp; funds its own AI data centres, chips (MTIA) and Superintelligence Labs from advertising
actors.advantage: Meta funds the build-out from an advertising business ($64.6bn of revenue a quarter) and buys talent outright: $14.3bn into Scale AI and packages reported up to $300m. Its chief says he would rather misspend hundreds of billions than be late.

actors.name: Oracle
actors.advantage: Oracle's durable base is its database and enterprise applications, which customers rarely leave because their systems are built on them. On that cash flow it bet on building OpenAI's Stargate capacity to order: $664bn of booked backlog, much of it one customer's $300bn contract, and $28.5bn of capex in one quarter, so its new advantage is also its risk.

actors.name: CoreWeave
actors.role: the largest independent GPU cloud, renting NVIDIA capacity to Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic
actors.advantage: CoreWeave turned early NVIDIA allocation into long rental contracts and a backlog near $100bn. But it borrowed about $35.1bn against those contracts and is valued at only $25.59bn: speed without a lasting moat.
actors.desire: Stay the neutral GPU landlord and refinance cheaply.
actors.fear: A customer that cuts or delays, rising debt costs, and GPUs that age before they pay back.

actors.name: Alibaba
actors.role: China's largest cloud and the maker of Qwen, a leading open-weight model family; also China's largest e-commerce group
actors.advantage: Alibaba Cloud is China's largest, its open Qwen models spread its platform, and it buys Huawei's chips where NVIDIA's are barred. Its position rests on China's protected market.
actors.desire: Lead China's AI cloud and models.
actors.fear: Chip supply, and price wars with ByteDance and Tencent.

actors.name: OpenAI
actors.advantage: ChatGPT is the default consumer AI brand: more than 900 million weekly users, over 50 million subscribers and 55.5% of chatbot web traffic in August 2026, down from 73.3% in summer 2025 as Gemini and Claude grew. OpenAI turned that audience into the largest private compute buyer, with contracts at Microsoft, Oracle, AWS, CoreWeave, NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom. The advantage is real but financed: revenue must keep growing to pay the commitments.

actors.name: Anthropic
actors.advantage: Anthropic grew its run-rate from about $9bn to over $47bn in five months by selling to enterprises and developers (over 1,000 customers each spend $1m a year), and buys compute on three chip platforms from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and xAI so no single supplier holds it. Its edge is revenue quality and a hedged compute plan.

actors.name: xAI
actors.role: Grok and the Colossus data centres; merged into SpaceX in 2026

actors.name: DeepSeek
actors.role: China's leading open-weight model lab, owned and funded by the hedge fund High-Flyer
actors.advantage: It releases near-frontier models free under the MIT licence, trained and served cheaply, and tuned its V4 to Huawei's Ascend chips. Its counter-position is price: closed labs must justify charging for what DeepSeek gives away.
actors.desire: Frontier capability at a fraction of the cost, and a public listing.
actors.fear: Compute limits from export controls, and rivals closing access after distillation accusations.

actors.name: SpaceX
actors.role: rockets (the lowest cost to orbit), the Starlink satellite network and, since 2026, xAI; listed in June 2026

actors.name: Palantir
actors.role: sells AI software (AIP, Foundry, Gotham) that governments and companies run on their own data
actors.advantage: Deployments embedded in defence and enterprise operations create high switching costs, and its security clearances are hard for rivals to obtain. The market prices it for perfection.
actors.desire: Be the operating system for AI in government and industry.
actors.fear: Budget cuts, a de-rating, and model makers moving into its niche.

actors.name: Consumers
actors.role: households that buy devices, subscriptions, medicines and goods, and whose attention advertisers buy
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the final source of most revenue in the chain. Its power is choice, which network effects and switching costs restrain.
actors.desire: Better products for less.
actors.fear: Inflation, job loss and higher energy bills.

actors.name: Enterprises
actors.role: companies that buy cloud, AI and advertising, including the AI natives, utilities and developers that buy chips and power
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the business demand on which the clouds' revenue rests.
actors.desire: Productivity from AI at falling cost.
actors.fear: Paying for AI that does not pay back.

actors.name: Governments
actors.role: public buyers of AI software, defence systems and sovereign AI clusters
actors.advantage: Not a firm: a buyer whose orders follow security and policy rather than price.
actors.desire: Sovereign AI capability.
actors.fear: Dependence on foreign suppliers.

actors.name: Venture funds
actors.role: the venture, growth and sovereign funds that finance private AI labs
actors.advantage: Not a firm: the risk capital of an open economy. In 2026 it is one bet: AI took 82.7% of a record $515.8bn of US venture deal value.
actors.desire: Back the next winner.
actors.fear: A closed exit window and marks that fall.

actors.name: US government
actors.role: the rule of law, the patent system, export controls and the dollar; through the Federal Reserve, the price of money
actors.advantage: It sets the environment the chain stands on: courts and patents, deep capital markets, export licences that decide who abroad may buy advanced chips and tools, and a 9.9% stake in Intel. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75-4% in October 2026, with two members wanting a rise.
actors.desire: AI leadership over China, chip making at home, and growth without inflation.
actors.fear: Losing the AI race, a Taiwan crisis, and inflation from oil and tariffs.

actors.name: Taiwan
actors.role: home of TSMC's leading-edge fabs: the single place where most advanced chips are made
actors.advantage: It hosts most of the world's advanced chip making, a 'silicon shield' that gives the US and others a stake in its security.
actors.desire: Stay indispensable.
actors.fear: A blockade or attack from China.

actors.name: EU
actors.role: the single market and its regulators (the AI Act, competition law); home of ASML's supply base
actors.advantage: Market size and rule-making: firms everywhere adapt to its rules, but it has few AI champions of its own.
actors.desire: Sovereign AI and chip capacity.
actors.fear: Dependence on US clouds and Asian fabs.

actors.name: Netherlands
actors.role: home of ASML; its export licences decide which lithography tools reach China
actors.advantage: It holds the licence over the one EUV maker, so it is a lever in US-China technology policy.
actors.desire: Keep ASML at home and its trade open.
actors.fear: Being squeezed between Washington and Beijing.

actors.name: South Korea
actors.role: home of SK Hynix and Samsung: most of the world's high-bandwidth memory
actors.advantage: It holds most HBM capacity, so every AI accelerator depends on its fabs.
actors.desire: Keep the memory lead and build foundry share.
actors.fear: China's memory makers, and US-China decoupling squeezing its exports.

actors.name: Japan
actors.role: home of Tokyo Electron, SoftBank and key chip materials such as photoresists and wafers
actors.advantage: Near-monopolies in chip materials and coater-developer tools; it backs a new leading-edge foundry (Rapidus).
actors.desire: Rebuild a leading-edge chip industry.
actors.fear: Dependence on Taiwan and an older, shrinking workforce.

actors.name: Gulf states
actors.role: oil exporters and sovereign investors (Aramco, MGX); the Strait of Hormuz runs past them

actors.name: Mastercard
actors.advantage: Visa's twin in a duopoly: the same two-sided network economics, with a toll on each card payment.
actors.desire: Be the default rail for new payments, including agent-initiated ones.
actors.fear: Fee regulation and account-to-account payments.

actors.name: ExxonMobil
actors.advantage: Integrated scale in oil, gas, refining and chemicals, and low-cost Permian and Guyana barrels; it gains from the 2026 oil shock without the Gulf's exposure to Hormuz.
actors.desire: Grow low-cost production and keep buying back shares.
actors.fear: An oil price collapse when the war ends, and demand loss to electrification.

actors.name: J&J
actors.advantage: A diversified portfolio of patented drugs and medical devices, with a balance sheet that buys new drugs as old patents expire.
actors.desire: Replace expiring drug franchises.
actors.fear: Patent cliffs and US drug-price controls.

actors.name: Tesla
actors.advantage: What remains is its brand, which still lets it price above rivals and carries a $1.415 trillion valuation, and the driving data of its fleet for self-driving software. Its cost lead in cars has passed to BYD (Q3 2026: 486,532 deliveries against BYD's 762,478) and its operating margin fell to 2.6%, so its value is now a bet on autonomy and robots.

actors.name: BYD
actors.advantage: BYD makes its own batteries (it is also one of the largest battery makers), power chips and motors, so it builds each car at a lower cost than rivals that buy them; that integrated process and its volume made it the largest battery-electric seller, with 762,478 cars in Q3 2026 against Tesla's 486,532. Rivals would need years of investment across the whole supply chain to match its cost.

actors.name: Jin dynasty
actors.role: the Jurchen state of northern China that the Mongols besieged from 1211

actors.name: Khwarazm
actors.role: the Central Asian empire the Mongols destroyed in 1219-1221

actors.name: Baby Bells
actors.role: the regional operating companies created by the Bell System's break-up in 1984

actors.name: Standard's heirs
actors.role: the 34 companies created by Standard Oil's dissolution in 1911, among them the ancestors of Exxon, Mobil and Chevron

chokepoints.alternatives: Mastercard; account-to-account payments and stablecoins at the margin
Bing (4.8%); AI assistants such as ChatGPT are the first real substitute

chokepoints.share: output larger than the next nine manufacturing countries combined
chokepoints.alternatives: Vietnam, India and Mexico for assembly; years to replace for batteries and refined materials

chokepoints.controls: export licences for advanced AI chips, chipmaking tools and design software

chokepoints.alternatives: for China, Huawei's Ascend and domestic tools, generations behind

flashpoints.title: CUDA against the second sources
flashpoints.mechanism: Every framework, library and engineer is tuned to CUDA, so AMD and the TPU win only where a buyer can rewrite its stack and wants a second source.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA keeps about 75% of accelerators, down from about 87% in 2024, while AMD's data-centre revenue reached a record $8.5bn and Broadcom's AI revenue $16.7bn in a quarter.

flashpoints.title: The TPU bypass
flashpoints.advantage: its own chip, designed with Broadcom
flashpoints.mechanism: A hyperscaler that owns its workloads designs its own accelerator with Broadcom and sells the capacity, avoiding NVIDIA's margin in a way NVIDIA cannot answer without cutting it.
flashpoints.outcome: Just over half of Google's ML compute goes to TPUs, with 4.3 million TPU shipments projected for 2026, and Anthropic took 3.5 GW of Broadcom-built TPU capacity from 2027 plus 5 GW from Google Cloud.

flashpoints.title: AMD buys its way in
flashpoints.mechanism: Buyers who want a second source take AMD's MI450 on large commitments, and AMD pays for the switch with warrants and lower margins.
flashpoints.outcome: OpenAI committed 6 GW with warrants for up to 160m AMD shares, Meta 6 GW in an estimated $60bn deal, and AMD's data-centre revenue rose 97% to $8.5bn in Q3 2026.

flashpoints.title: Memory earns more than NVIDIA
flashpoints.advantage: the scarcest input, sold out to 2029
flashpoints.mechanism: HBM capacity could not grow as fast as accelerators, so memory makers sold out for years and NVIDIA committed capital to secure supply.
flashpoints.outcome: SK Hynix's operating profit was 83.33 of 104.6 trillion won of revenue (about 80%), above NVIDIA's 66%, and NVIDIA's purchase commitments rose from $119bn to $279bn.

flashpoints.title: HBM: SK Hynix against Samsung
flashpoints.mechanism: SK Hynix qualified its HBM with NVIDIA first and locked in long contracts, while Samsung used its larger DRAM capacity to catch up as HBM4 ramped.
flashpoints.outcome: SK Hynix held 50% of HBM in Q2 2026, down from 64% a year earlier, while Samsung rose from 21% to 33% in one quarter and Micron held 18%.

flashpoints.title: EUV: one machine, one maker
flashpoints.mechanism: Only ASML can build EUV systems, so every leading-edge fab must buy from it, and export rules can switch China off.
flashpoints.outcome: ASML reported record Q3 2026 net sales of EUR 11.7bn and says supply for 2027 and 2028 will not meet demand, while China buys only older DUV tools.

flashpoints.title: TSMC against Intel and Samsung
flashpoints.advantage: yield at the leading edge, and trust
flashpoints.mechanism: Customers design for TSMC first because only it delivers leading-edge yield at volume, and as a pure foundry it never competes with them.
flashpoints.outcome: TSMC took 72.5% of top-10 foundry revenue in Q2 2026 against Samsung's 5.9% and SMIC's 5.4%, with a 66.4% gross margin, while Intel needed the US government (9.9%) and NVIDIA ($5bn) as owners.

flashpoints.title: China shuts NVIDIA out
flashpoints.advantage: state control of a large market
flashpoints.mechanism: After Washington allowed H200 sales, Beijing told customs to block them and steered its firms to Huawei's Ascend, so its market became a protected home for its own chips.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA's China share fell to zero by its CEO's account and its guidance assumes no China data-centre compute, while Huawei expects about $12bn of AI-chip revenue in 2026, up from $7.5bn.

flashpoints.title: Export controls against China
flashpoints.advantage: control of the chain's choke points
flashpoints.mechanism: The US and its allies deny China EUV tools and the best accelerators, so Chinese chips stay generations behind and must be made on older DUV machines.
flashpoints.outcome: SMIC makes Huawei's chips without EUV at a 5.4% foundry share, and China still bought 23% of ASML's Q3 equipment sales (about EUR 1.93bn) in older DUV tools.

flashpoints.title: Chips for equity
flashpoints.mechanism: NVIDIA invests in its customers (OpenAI, Anthropic, CoreWeave, Intel) so they can keep buying its systems, and AMD answers with warrants.
flashpoints.outcome: NVIDIA offered up to $100bn to OpenAI and up to $10bn to Anthropic, put $2bn into CoreWeave at $87.20 a share, and AMD offered OpenAI warrants for up to 160m shares.

flashpoints.title: Oracle wins OpenAI's biggest contract
flashpoints.mechanism: When Microsoft gave up exclusivity, Oracle won OpenAI's largest compute contract by building to order and carrying the cost on its own balance sheet.
flashpoints.outcome: OpenAI agreed to buy $300bn of compute from Oracle over five years, Oracle's backlog reached $664bn, and it spent $28.5bn of capex in one quarter.

flashpoints.title: Anthropic against OpenAI
flashpoints.mechanism: Anthropic sold to enterprises and developers and bought compute on three chip platforms as revenue arrived, while OpenAI built on consumer scale and very large commitments.
flashpoints.outcome: Anthropic's run-rate rose from about $9bn to over $47bn by May 2026 and its valuation ($965bn) passed OpenAI's ($852bn), whose run-rate was about $50bn in October.

flashpoints.title: Google absorbs the ChatGPT shock
flashpoints.mechanism: Google answered ChatGPT by building Gemini into its search, phones and cloud on its own TPUs, accepting the cost to its search margin rather than leaving the field to a new rival.
flashpoints.outcome: Google still held 91.05% of search in October 2026 and Gemini took 25.6% of chatbot traffic, while ChatGPT's share fell from 73.3% to 55.5% even as it reached 900 million weekly users.

flashpoints.title: Open weights against closed labs
flashpoints.mechanism: DeepSeek releases near-frontier models free under the MIT licence and runs them cheaply on Chinese chips, so closed labs must justify charging for what it gives away.
flashpoints.outcome: DeepSeek released the 1.6-trillion-parameter V4-Pro in April 2026 and was valued at $52bn in May, against Anthropic's $965bn, and Anthropic accused it of distilling Claude.

flashpoints.title: The talent auction
flashpoints.mechanism: Meta used its advertising cash to buy researchers outright, with packages reported up to $300m and a $14.3bn stake in Scale AI to hire its founder.
flashpoints.outcome: Meta Superintelligence Labs grew to about 3,000 people and its Muse Spark model reached the top five of Artificial Analysis benchmarks in July 2026.

flashpoints.title: Cash flow against leverage
flashpoints.mechanism: Microsoft funds about $170bn a year of capex from operations, while Oracle and CoreWeave borrow against their customers' contracts to build.
flashpoints.outcome: Microsoft expects to stay free-cash-flow positive, while Oracle spent $28.5bn of capex in a quarter and CoreWeave carries about $35.1bn of debt against a $25.59bn market value.

flashpoints.title: The turbine queue
flashpoints.advantage: a full order book in a scarce product
flashpoints.mechanism: Data centres need firm power faster than grids can add it, and only three firms make large gas turbines, so buyers reserve slots years ahead.
flashpoints.outcome: GE Vernova's gas backlog and slot reservations reached 122 GW, heading for at least 130 GW, and its Q3 2026 orders rose 96% to $29bn.

flashpoints.title: GLP-1: Lilly passes Novo
flashpoints.advantage: a better drug, made at volume
flashpoints.mechanism: Novo made the obesity market, but Lilly's tirzepatide worked better and Lilly scaled supply faster, so it took the growth.
flashpoints.outcome: Lilly's Q3 2026 revenue rose 39% to $24.40bn and it guides $91-92bn for the year, while Novo guides 2026 sales growth of -2% to +2%.

flashpoints.title: BYD out-builds Tesla
flashpoints.mechanism: BYD makes its own batteries and chips and builds cars at a cost Tesla cannot match, so Tesla moves its story to autonomy and robots.
flashpoints.outcome: In Q3 2026 BYD sold 762,478 battery-electric cars to Tesla's 486,532, and Tesla's operating margin fell to 2.6%, though Tesla is still valued at $1.415 trillion against BYD's $116bn.

flashpoints.title: Trainium wins Anthropic
flashpoints.advantage: its own chip sold with its cloud
flashpoints.mechanism: Amazon designs Trainium and sells it with AWS capacity, so a lab that commits to AWS gets cheaper compute and Amazon keeps the margin NVIDIA would have taken.
flashpoints.outcome: In April 2026 Anthropic committed $100bn over ten years to Trainium and Graviton (5 GW), alongside up to $25bn of new Amazon investment, while AWS grew 39% to $46.0bn a quarter.

flashpoints.title: Microsoft hedges its OpenAI bet
flashpoints.advantage: a stake in one lab, a channel for all
flashpoints.mechanism: Microsoft kept about 27% of OpenAI and a large Azure commitment while investing in Anthropic and selling Claude, so it earns whichever lab wins its enterprise customers.
flashpoints.outcome: Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9bn in a quarter, up 30%, while OpenAI placed its largest new contracts with Oracle ($300bn over five years) and AWS ($38bn).

flashpoints.title: xAI rents Colossus to a rival
flashpoints.advantage: capacity built fast, with its own power
flashpoints.mechanism: xAI built its Colossus data centres faster than rivals could find power and sites, and now rents capacity to a competing lab like a GPU landlord.
flashpoints.outcome: Anthropic pays SpaceX's xAI $1.25bn a month for Colossus 1 through May 2029, while xAI's segment lost $6.4bn on $3.2bn of revenue in 2025.

flashpoints.title: Walmart's stores against Amazon
flashpoints.advantage: stores near every shopper, and their data
flashpoints.mechanism: Walmart turned its store network into fast delivery points and its shoppers' data into an advertising business, competing with Amazon on speed and on ad margin.
flashpoints.outcome: Walmart's global advertising grew 38% in a quarter and it is the world's second-largest company by revenue, while Amazon delivered over 1.5 billion items same-day or overnight in a quarter.

flashpoints.title: Seven leave OpenAI
flashpoints.mechanism: Seven OpenAI researchers left to found Anthropic, taking their knowledge of scaling and safety with them.
flashpoints.outcome: Five years later Anthropic was valued at $965bn, above OpenAI's $852bn.

flashpoints.title: AWS leads cloud
flashpoints.mechanism: Amazon turned its internal infrastructure into the first large public cloud and kept the lead by scale.
flashpoints.outcome: AWS held 31% of cloud infrastructure in Q1 2023 against Azure's 25% and Google Cloud's 11%.

flashpoints.title: Intel leaves DRAM
flashpoints.advantage: giving up a lost market in time
flashpoints.mechanism: When Japanese memory makers crushed DRAM margins, Intel moved its capital to the microprocessor that the PC market needed.
flashpoints.outcome: Grove took Intel out of memory, and the 386 made Intel the key supplier of the PC standard.

flashpoints.title: Meta buys its challengers
flashpoints.advantage: cash from a network buys the next network
flashpoints.mechanism: Facebook bought the young networks that could have replaced it before they grew large.
flashpoints.outcome: Instagram for about $1bn in 2012 and WhatsApp for $19bn in 2014.

notes: Sizes: every arena company has a verified market cap (companiesmarketcap.com, read 7 Nov 2026, a Saturday, so prices are Friday's close) or a private valuation, except Huawei, which is employee-owned and has no market value or valuation; it is drawn as unverified. DeepSeek, which the brief expected to have none, raised a Series A in May 2026 at $52bn post-money. xAI is sized at the $250bn fair value its board set before the February 2026 merger; SpaceX's $1.823 trillion market cap contains it, so the two sizes overlap. SMIC is sized by its Hong Kong listing. The Federal Reserve is folded into us-gov (its facts are cited there); public markets, AbbVie and the aggregates (hyperscalers, big-four-hyperscalers, ai-supply-chain, us-ai-startups, ai-clouds-enterprise-sovereign) are dropped and their flows re-pointed or removed. Rivers: NVIDIA does not name its customers, so the four hyperscalers' rivers into NVIDIA apply Bloomberg and Barclays' 2025 customer shares (15/14/12/11%) to NVIDIA's revenue annualised from Q2 FY2027; its ACIE segment is drawn from the enterprises aggregate (AI clouds, AI natives, enterprises and sovereigns). OpenAI's run-rate is split 60/40 between consumers and enterprises using OpenAI's March 2026 statement that enterprise was roughly 40% of revenue; enterprise has grown since. SoftBank's river (cumulative $64.6bn over 2025-26) overlaps the venture-funds river of OpenAI's $122bn 2026 round, which included SoftBank. Euro and won amounts are converted at the ECB reference rates of 6 November 2026. Not drawn, for want of a term or an amount: OpenAI's incremental $250bn Azure commitment, Anthropic's $30bn Azure commitment, NVIDIA's up-to-$100bn investment in OpenAI (paid per gigawatt deployed), Meta's estimated $60bn AMD deal and $21bn CoreWeave expansion, Anthropic's Google TPU and Broadcom capacity, and the clouds' payments for electricity: no fetchable source gives the data centres' power bill, so the only energy river is GE Vernova's revenue from utilities and developers. Unverified and left out: Anthropic's reported $65bn run-rate at the end of July 2026; any per-customer split of NVIDIA's 2026 revenue.
openQuestions: Should xAI stand apart from SpaceX in the arena, given that SpaceX's market cap contains it?
NVIDIA's revenue by named customer in 2026 is undisclosed; the rivers use 2025 analyst shares. Would the user prefer one aggregated 'hyperscalers' river drawn as an estimate instead?
The data centres' payments for power have no sourced amount; should the power wall be shown by GE Vernova's backlog in GW rather than by a river?
OpenAI's $250bn Azure commitment has no disclosed term; when OpenAI or Microsoft discloses one, it becomes the largest lab-to-cloud river.
Altitude reads durable advantage, not momentum: Anthropic's valuation ($965bn) is above OpenAI's ($852bn) while its judged altitude is lower. Is that the reading the user wants the hillside to make?
